flawed_step: Step 2 of the proof attempt. Step 1 is fine: take distinct points x and y in a T1 space X. Because {x} and {y} are closed, U = X\{y} is an open set containing x and V = X\{x} is an open set containing y. Step 2 fails: it claims these sets, or some other open sets built from the T1 property, are disjoint. U ∩ V = X\{x,y}, which is non-empty whenever X has more than two points. Being T1 only guarantees open sets that leave out one chosen point. It never gives disjoint open sets, so this step cannot be justified.
counterexample: Give the natural numbers ℕ the cofinite topology, where the open sets are the empty set and the sets with finite complement. Every finite set is closed, so singletons are closed and the space is T1. Now take any two non-empty open sets U and V. Their complements are finite, so the complement of U ∩ V is finite too. Since ℕ is infinite, U ∩ V is not empty. So no two distinct points have disjoint neighbourhoods, and the space is not Hausdorff.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. The natural attempt uses the T1 property to get the open sets X\{y} (containing x) and X\{x} (containing y). Their intersection is X\{x,y}, which is non-empty as soon as X has more than two points, so the step claiming disjointness fails. The cofinite topology on an infinite set confirms this: it is T1, but any two non-empty open sets meet, so it is not Hausdorff.
